1.pericope_label: The fool hath said in his heart

schools.summary: Augustine reads the whole psalm out of its title: Maeleth, in the interpretations of Hebrew names, means for one travailing or in pain, and who travails in this world the faithful acknowledge, since they are that person — Christ travails here, the Head above and the members below, for one not in pain would not say, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me.

Calvin thinks a distinct commentary unnecessary, the psalm being almost identical with the fourteenth, and will not decide whether the variations came from transcribers or from a prophetic bard adapting it to a later distress — Theodoret referring it to Sennacherib's invasion under Hezekiah, others to the captivity. Gill notes the Targum's gloss, that there is no God of whom is revenge.

Henry, having expounded the psalm before, confines himself to three observations on sin — its fact, proved by an unexceptionable witness who sees all the sinfulness of men's lives naked and open; its fault, being iniquity in which there is no good; and its fountain, that there is no fear of God before their eyes, since bad practices flow from bad principles. Spurgeon spells out the denial: no God means no law, no order, no restraint to lust, and what a Bedlam, or rather what an Aceldama, the world would become if such principles were universal.

Clarke sends the reader back to his notes on the fourteenth psalm, adding only short remarks, and canvasses the renderings of the word in the title — the president, the leader of the dance, hollow instruments, the chorus — before preferring a flute.

Ellicott marks the wanting conjunction and the substitution of iniquity for the general term doings, as though the adapter felt a word applicable to good as well as evil too weak for such profanity; Keil and Delitzsch call the change more bombastic, note the dropped asyndeton, and argue from the levelling of the divine names — seven times Elohim here where the older psalm mingles Elohim and Jahve deliberately — that David cannot himself have made the change.

debates.question: Where do the differences from the fourteenth psalm come from?

sides.position: either transcribers or a later bard adapting the psalm to a fresh distress — Theodoret naming Sennacherib, others the captivity
a deliberate reviser, since the levelling of the divine names is carried out more rigidly than the Elohimic character demands, and cannot be David’s own

themes: a recension of the fourteenth psalm

4.pericope_label: Where no fear was: the variant ending

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the sense where the others weigh letters — none of the workers of iniquity lack knowledge unless given up to judicial blindness — and reads the closing wish forward, as the church's desire for Christ's coming in the latter day to destroy antichrist and deliver his people, taking the plural salvations for the complete salvation of the church.

Clarke counts the seventy-two manuscripts that restore the omitted 'all', reads the added words of the fifth verse as levelled at the Babylonians who sacked Jerusalem and were sacked in their turn, and sends the reader to Kennicott's Hebrew Bible where the variations of the two psalms are exhibited at one view. Wesley has God not only breaking the enemy's strength but dispersing them beyond hope of restoration.

Ellicott calls 'where no fear was' the most interesting variation, plainly inserted to suit some circumstance we have no clue to, excludes the reading that takes fear in a good sense, and would render it where there was no cause for fear — said, from the context, of Israel itself rather than its enemies. Keil and Delitzsch reject the theory that the closing lines are a restoration of a faded manuscript, since they sound too complete and full of life, and ascribe them to a later poet adapting the psalm to a catastrophe of his own day.

debates.question: Of whom is "there were they in great fear" spoken?

sides.position: of Israel itself, a people supposed to live under God’s protection yet liable to sudden panics
of the Babylonians, the added words being levelled at the sackers of Jerusalem

themes: who eat up my people as bread
there were they in great fear
the bones of him that encampeth
the salvation of Israel out of Zion
